related_questions.question: What is an example of a killed vaccine?

text_blocks.snippet: Killed or inactivated vaccines use pathogens that have been killed (usually through heat or chemicals) to prevent them from causing disease, while still triggering an immune response. Examples include the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), some influenza vaccines, hepatitis A vaccine, and rabies vaccine. These vaccines are generally considered safer for immunocompromised individuals because they cannot replicate and cause infection.
snippet_highlighted_words: inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), some influenza vaccines, hepatitis A vaccine, and rabies vaccine

list.title: How they work:
list.snippet: Inactivated vaccines contain pathogens that have been killed or rendered inactive. This means the pathogen cannot replicate or cause disease, but the immune system can still recognize its components (like proteins or antigens) as foreign and develop an immune response.
Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV): This vaccine uses killed polio viruses to protect against polio.
Influenza Vaccines: Most flu shots are made with inactivated influenza viruses.
Hepatitis A Vaccine: This vaccine protects against hepatitis A by using an inactivated form of the virus.
Rabies Vaccine: The rabies vaccine is another example of a killed vaccine.

list.title: Advantages:
list.snippet: Inactivated vaccines are generally safer for people with weakened immune systems because they cannot cause the disease they are designed to prevent.

list.title: Disadvantages:
list.snippet: They may require multiple doses to provide sufficient immunity and might not induce as long-lasting or robust protection as live attenuated vaccines.
